extracted.intended_audience: news consumers and journalists interested in media accountability and investigative reporting
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative considerations for producing and assessing investigative audio journalism (podcasts) with emphasis on source verification, editorial oversight, accuracy, and transparency, as illustrated by The New York Times' Caliphate case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and fact-checking standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The series did not meet its standards for accuracy or fact-checking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Times posted an editor's note saying the series should never have been produced with Chaudhry as a central character; parts about Chaudhry were effectively retracted. Editors must ensure reporting meets institutional accuracy and fact-checking standards before publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification of source claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters failed to push hard enough to verify Chaudhry's claims; the paper did not have evidence he had ever been to Syria, joined ISIS, or killed civilians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require 'powerful evidence' to justify extraordinary claims. Do not accept a subject's account at face value—seek independent documentary, testimonial, or other corroboration that can substantiate travel, membership in organizations, or involvement in crimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroboration from independent evidence and officials
rubrics_metrics.description: Corroboration relied on colleagues' and officials' suspicions, but it wasn't clear whether those officials relied on hard evidence or the subject's own claims on social media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When citing intelligence or official views, confirm whether those views are based on hard evidence. Distinguish between official suspicion and verifiable proof; document the basis for claims drawn from third-party authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overreliance on a single compelling source
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and reporters 'fell in love' with having a member of ISIS describe crimes; when evidence arose that he might be a fabulist, the team 'didn't listen hard enough.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of narrative temptation — a compelling single source should not drive the story without independent verification. Maintain skepticism even when a source appears to deliver exclusive, vivid material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial skepticism and oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Top editors were deferential to an ambitious audio investigative team and to the reporter's authority rather than pushing harder to verify the central claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should apply the same rigorous skepticism and verification standards to audio teams as to written investigative desks. Do not defer editorial judgment solely on the basis of a reporter's reputation; actively challenge assumptions and demand proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about errors, corrections, and retractions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Times publicly acknowledged the failures, posted editor's notes, and offered to return awards; Baquet: 'When we get it wrong, I want people to understand we're going to talk about it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting proves unreliable, be transparent: publish corrections or editor's notes, explain what failed, and communicate steps taken. Consider formal retractions for core factual failures and, where appropriate, return awards or notify awarding bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal review and accountability processes
rubrics_metrics.description: A separate internal review found repeated failures to verify; the paper reassigned the reporter and said the review could yield additional corrections of past work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement independent internal reviews when serious errors emerge; use findings to correct the public record, re-evaluate related reporting, and determine personnel or process changes to prevent recurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist forcing narrative to fit conflicting evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The reporting team considered shifting dates and using an 'Occam's razor' approach to make pieces of the story fit together despite timeline contradictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not alter timelines or otherwise contort facts to preserve a preferred narrative. If evidence conflicts, report the contradictions transparently rather than reconciling them through speculative adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough interrogation of inconsistencies and subject credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when confronted with contradictions, the team sought ways to show the subject's story could still be true; the subject was later accused of being a fabulist and of lying to authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively interrogate and document inconsistencies in a subject's account; corroborate key claims independently; treat subjects who have made inconsistent or implausible prior claims with heightened scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awards and acclaim do not substitute for verification
rubrics_metrics.description: The series won awards (Peabody, Pulitzer finalist) yet core elements were later retracted when verification failed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let prestige, accolades, or institutional pride prevent re-examination of reporting. Use external recognition as neither proof nor a shield against critique; follow up on substantive challenges regardless of prior acclaim.
